activities.caption: pair each measure with the claim it carries
activities.name: netMeasuresMatch

config.prompt: Every measure is a claim about social life — pair them:

pairs.right: raw connectivity — whose distribution matters more than its average: a few hubs dominate flow
your friends know each other — the closure that builds trust and enforces norms
how often you sit on the shortest path between others — the broker's measure
weights connections by how well-connected your contacts are — the logic behind PageRank
the only edge between two clusters — novel information's channel, and the point where removal splits the network

config.why: The same vocabulary recurs through every result: weak ties and small worlds are bridge-and-path statements, contagion turns on clustering, brokerage restates as inequality — one machine, not four separate ideas.

activities.caption: order the small-world research arc
activities.name: netSmallOrder

config.prompt: From chain letters to scale-free hubs — order the arc:
items: Milgram's chain-letter experiment (1967): completed chains average roughly six intermediaries
The honest reading: only about a fifth of chains completed — the successful ones by construction
Watts and Strogatz (1998): rewire a small fraction of a lattice's edges at random
A tiny rewiring probability collapses path length while clustering barely drops — the small-world recipe
Barabási and Albert's scale-free model: preferential attachment builds the hubs
config.why: The lesson generalises: diseases traverse the planet in weeks, rumours outrun corrections, and network interventions (targeting hubs, cutting bridges) beat population-average ones.

config.prompt: What spreads on one exposure, and what needs reinforcement? File each:

items.label: behaviours with social risk or effort — multiple reinforcing exposures from distinct sources

config.why: The reversal is the finding: wide bridges that carry information well can be too narrow to carry behaviour — information spreads along weak ties, behaviour through redundant reinforcement.

activities.caption: true or false — the echo-chamber claim
activities.name: netEchoJudge

statements.why: But the measured facts complicate the headline, not confirm it.

statements.s: Online ideological segregation is entirely manufactured by the algorithm.
statements.why: It is substantially a pre-existing feature of whom people choose to connect with — and varies enormously by platform and topic.

statements.s: In some datasets, online segregation exceeds what choice-based models predict offline.
statements.why: Which is exactly why the causal responsibility of the algorithm is genuinely contested.

statements.s: The network-structure facts are solid; the causal story is a live research fight.
statements.why: Not a settled headline — the identification work is still running.

activities.anchor: has structural variants with different payoffs
activities.caption: drag between bonding and bridging
activities.name: netCapitalCompare

config.prompt: Two kinds of social capital, two payoffs — drag the divider:

before.label: Bonding
before.text: Dense, closed, similar networks (Coleman's closure): support, trust enforcement, norms — and the same closure that enforces norms enforces surveillance. What families and tight communities provide.

after.label: Bridging
after.text: Spanning, heterogeneous ties across structural holes: novel information and opportunity — brokers consistently promoted faster and paid more, everything else held constant.

config.why: Putnam's Bowling Alone documented the aggregate decline of US civic connectedness — and the distinction explains why its prescriptions are hard: the policies that build one are not those that build the other.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the inequality plumbing
activities.name: netPlumbingSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is wrong — click it:
lines: Jobs, information and norms flow through ties.
DiTomaso found advantage operating through favoritism rather than exclusion.
Reproducing inequality through networks requires an intended bigot.
A segregated network is a small world within each group and a large world across groups.
Opportunity hoards through the plumbing of who knows whom.
config.correction: No intent is required: ordinary in-group helping — people assist those they know, along networks built by prior advantage — reproduces stratification.
config.why: The structure of who knows whom — not just who intends what — carries the water where it was laid.

activities.anchor: A closing note connects this chapter
activities.caption: drag between the pipe and the water
activities.name: netPipeCompare

config.prompt: The dual literacy — drag the divider:

before.label: The pipe
before.text: Structure measured carefully: degree, betweenness, bridges — formal measures that are meaningless without the cultural content of ties: what a 'friend' is, what obligation a favour carries.

after.label: The water
after.text: Meaning studied seriously — and unreadable without the structure, since who is connected to whom constrains what meanings can travel.

config.why: The strongest work holds both, with the causal-identification problems named rather than laundered — which is why network analysis has migrated so successfully into epidemiology, economics and organisational research.
